title: Flash Eurobarometer 578
text:
European Commission: Growing use of AI in European companies

WhoEuropean Commission, DG EMPL
When2026
WhereEU-27
SampleFirms12,826 SMEs and mid-caps (1 to 749 employees)
AI useFirmAI and algorithmic management in the workplace, asked as one item, so
the two cannot be separated
QuestionDoes the company use AI or algorithmic management, and what drives or
holds back adoption?
DemographicsFirmssize class (1-9 to 250-749), sector, turnover, country, in-house or external supplier, supplier location (EU or not)
AdoptionFirms: 42%

Main aim. To identify what drives and what hinders the adoption of AI and
algorithmic management in smaller companies, with a focus on workplace
issues.Also covers. Workforce uses (recruitment, HR decisions, performance monitoring,
scheduling, health and safety, training), human oversight, expected
effects on job quality (job satisfaction, safety, privacy, workload),
employees’ reactions as seen by employers, motivations such as labour
shortages, and barriers. No questions on employment or productivity
effects.

text:

2026)

WhoEuropean Commission, DG ECFIN
When2026
Where18 EU Member States

tasks, or both
Question“Are you using AI technologies for your work or for personal tasks?”
DemographicsIndividualsage, sex, education, occupation, full-time or part-time, household income quartile, country

quality of work, workload and fear of job loss. The core survey covers

text:

title: EIB Investment Survey
text:
EIB Investment Survey 2025: European Union overview

WhoEuropean Investment Bank
When2025
WhereEU-27 (plus a US sample)
SampleFirms12,033 firms
AI useFirmUse by the firm, not by individual workers
QuestionTwo questions combined: whether the firm has implemented “Big data
analytics and artificial intelligence”, and “I would like to ask about
your company’s systematic use of generative AI tools to improve
processes. […] Does your company invest in these kinds of tools in any
of the following areas?”
DemographicsFirmssize, sector, country, turnover, employment, wage bill, exporter or importer, female ownership and management
AdoptionFirms: 37% (EIB measure of firms using generative AI, built from a big data and AI
question and a generative AI investment question; weighted by value
added. Not comparable with the 2026 wave)

Main aim. To track firms’ investment activity, financing needs and obstacles to
investment across the EU. Generative AI was added as part of the section
on digital technologies.Also covers. Investment by asset type (including training of employees), obstacles to
investment such as a shortage of staff with the right skills, access to
finance, innovation and digitalisation, climate investment and trade.

The EIB labels this chart “Firms using generative AI”, and the note under it lists two questions: whether the firm uses big data analytics and artificial intelligence, and whether it invests in generative AI tools (overview, p. 27). The EIB does not say how the two answers are combined. The sector figures suggest a firm must answer yes to both: 39% of manufacturing firms and 36% of service firms are counted here, while 48% and 41% use big data and AI (p. 25), and a measure counting a yes to either question could not be lower than that. Shares are weighted by value added (“About this publication”), whereas Eurostat’s 20% for 2025 counts each firm equally; Bick et al. find that reweighting Eurostat’s data by value added gives levels close to the EIBIS ones (St. Louis Fed Working Paper 2026-003B, Section 3.2 and Appendix C.1; the NBER version, w34995, does not include this comparison).

title: Bick et al.
text:
Bick, Blandin, Deming, Fuchs-Schündeln and Jessen: Mind the Gap: AI
Adoption in Europe and the U.S.

WhoBick, Blandin, Deming, Fuchs-Schündeln and Jessen (academic survey)
When2025
WhereGermany, France, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden (plus UK and US)

Question“Do you use Generative AI for your job?”
DemographicsWorkersage, sex, education, income, occupation, industry, hours worked, establishment size, country

Main aim. To measure generative AI use at work in a way that is comparable between
the United States and Europe, using the same questionnaire in every

used for, and reasons for not using it.

title: JRC AIM-WORK
text:
JRC: Digital monitoring, algorithmic management and the platformisation
of work in Europe

WhoEuropean Commission, JRC and DG EMPL

WhereEU-27

Question“In the last 12 months, did you use an AI-powered tool when performing

title: Eurofound EWCS
text:
Eurofound: EWCS 2024 first findings

WhoEurofound
When2024
Where35 European countries
SampleWorkers36,644 people
AI useAt workUse for work only
Question“And do you use the following equipment in your work? […] Artificial
Intelligence that simplifies complex mental tasks or makes
recommendations on how you should be working? (ChatGPT, LLAMA, DALL-E,
Midjourney, Jasper)”
DemographicsWorkersage, sex, education, occupation (ISCO 4-digit), contract type, working hours, earnings, migrant background, tenure, countryFirmsworkplace size (reported by worker), sector (NACE), employment change over 3 years, worker representation
AdoptionWorkers: 12% (workers, all ages)

Main aim. To monitor working conditions and job quality across Europe. The AI
question is one item in a long questionnaire on tasks, autonomy, work
intensity and health.Also covers. The seven job-quality indices (physical and social environment, working
time, work intensity, skills and discretion, prospects, earnings),
algorithmic management, training, health and well-being, telework and
work-life balance.
12% of EU workers use generative AI tools at work. Among EU countries the share runs from 5% or less in Greece, Italy, Portugal and Romania to at least one in five in Luxembourg, Sweden, Belgium and Denmark (Eurofound overview report, pp. 27-28). Across all 35 countries surveyed, the range is from under 3% (Bosnia-Herzegovina) to about 25% (Luxembourg).

title: EU-OSHA ESENER
text:
EU-OSHA: ESENER 2024 first findings

WhoEU-OSHA

title: Country evidence
text: National surveys with their own AI questions, from central banks, statistical offices and research institutes, and national releases of the Eurostat surveys where they add regional detail or newer data. They cover one country each, so they are not plotted on the overview. The label after each name says what the AI question covers: use at work, use for work and in private life (asked separately), use for any purpose, or use by the firm.

title: Country evidence
text:
Germany
ifo Business Survey Firm · ifo Institute · May 2026 · Firms, about 9,000. Asks whether AI is in use, planned, under discussion, or not an issue.

Bundesbank Online Panel Firms Firm · Deutsche Bundesbank, Monthly Report March 2026, box “Generative AI in German enterprises: adoption, costs and expected economic impact” (pp. 109-110) · April to June 2025 · Firms, more than 7,000. “Has your enterprise already used generative artificial intelligence (AI) or is it planning to use it in future?”, asked for 2024, 2025 and 2026.

Bundesbank Online Panel Firms, 2026 waves Firm · Deutsche Bundesbank, reported in Yotzov et al., NBER Working Paper 34836 (revised October 2026) · January and July 2026 · Firms, about 2,500 in January and about 2,300 in July; results weighted by employment. “Which of the following artificial intelligence technologies, if any, does your business currently use?”, from a list that includes generative AI and machine learning; the list changed slightly between the two waves. Both values are from Figure A4 of the October 2026 revision. The question differs from the 2025 module above, so the two are not comparable. Weighting by employment gives large firms more weight and raises the share, so it is not comparable with the firm shares of ifo or the establishment shares of IAB either; the authors find that weighting, firm size and who answers each move measured adoption by five to twelve percentage points (p. 15).

IAB Establishment Panel Firm · Institute for Employment Research · July to November 2025 · Firms, about 15,000 establishments of all sizes. Asks whether the establishment uses generative AI, and since when.

DiWaBe 2.0 At work · BAuA, ZEW, IAB and BIBB · July to December 2024 · Workers, 9,835 employees aged 16 to 65. “How often do you work with AI-supported computer programs?”

title: Country evidence
text:
France
Monthly business survey, AI module Firm · Banque de France · 25 February to 3 April 2026 · Firms, about 7,000; results for those with 20+ employees. Asks what use the firm makes of generative and non-generative AI: intensive, limited, experimental, planned, or none.

ICT survey of enterprises 2025 Firm · INSEE, Insee Première 2120 · first quarter of 2025 · Firms, a sample of 11,000 from about 194,000 enterprises with 10+ employees in mainly market sectors, excluding agriculture, finance and insurance. Asks whether the enterprise uses any of eight AI technologies; this is the French part of the Eurostat survey, and the figures are the same as Eurostat’s for France.

title: Country evidence
text:
Italy
Survey of Industrial and Service Firms Firm · Banca d’Italia · 17 February to 12 May 2026 · Firms, about 4,000 with 20+ employees. Asks what use the firm makes of predictive and generative AI: extensive, limited, experimental, planned, or none.

Survey on Inflation and Growth Expectations (SIGE) Firm · Banca d’Italia, reported in Ropele and Tagliabracci (2026), Questioni di Economia e Finanza 1005 · third quarter of 2024 · Firms, about 1,300 with 50+ employees in industry and non-financial private services (the roughly 200 construction firms in each wave were not asked the AI questions); results weighted. “How important is the use of artificial intelligence (e.g., cloud computing, predictive and/or generative artificial intelligence, robotics) to your company’s activities?” The examples include cloud computing and robotics, so the question is broader than AI alone.

Conjunctural Survey on Italian Households Any purpose · Banca d’Italia, reported in Loschiavo and Moscatelli (2025), Questioni di Economia e Finanza 929 · August to September 2024 · Individuals, a final sample of 1,916 households, surveyed online from the sample of the Survey on Household Income and Wealth. “How often have you used Gen AI tools in the past 12 months?”

title: Country evidence
text:
Spain
Business Activity Survey (EBAE) Firm · Banco de España · 11 to 25 November 2024 · Firms, about 6,300 of all sizes. Asks how much the firm uses predictive and generative AI: none, planned, sporadic or pilot, moderate, or high.

title: Country evidence
text:
Austria
AI use and attitudes Any purpose · Statistics Austria · April to July 2025 · Individuals, 5,550 people aged 16 to 74. Asks whether people have used AI tools to generate text, images or other content, and how often in the last three months.

title: Country evidence
text:
Netherlands
Belevingen 2025, AI module At work · Statistics Netherlands (CBS) · 23 January to 30 June 2025 · Individuals, 3,834 adults aged 18+; the work question goes to those in paid work. “Gebruikt u op dit moment kunstmatige intelligentie voor uw werk?” (Do you currently use artificial intelligence for your work?)

Employers’ Survey on Work (WEA) 2024 Firm · TNO · 15 January to 29 May 2024 · Firms, 3,460 establishments with 5+ employees. Asks which technologies the establishment uses, including “algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI) or big data techniques to improve processes, products or services”.

title: Country evidence
text:
Belgium
ICT usage in enterprises 2025 Firm · Statbel · 2025 · Firms, a sample of around 7,500 enterprises with 2+ persons employed; the figures here are for enterprises with 10+ persons employed in the standard Eurostat scope, so they equal Eurostat’s figures for Belgium. Asks whether the enterprise uses any of eight AI technologies; this is the Belgian part of the Eurostat survey, with regional results that Eurostat does not publish. In 2025, 28.8% of enterprises with 10 to 49 persons employed used AI, 54.5% of those with 50 to 249 and 76.4% of those with 250 or more.

ICT usage in households 2025 Work and private · Statbel · 2025 · Individuals aged 16 to 74. Asks whether people used generative AI tools in the last three months, and for what purpose; this is the Belgian part of the Eurostat survey. Of those who used it, 49.6% used it for professional purposes, and 67.5% of users who are in work.

title: Country evidence
text:
Denmark
AI chatbot adoption surveys Work and private · Humlum and Vestergaard, fielded by Statistics Denmark · November to December 2024 (first wave late 2023) · Workers, 25,241 in 11 AI-exposed occupations covering about a fifth of Danish employment. “Har du benyttet følgende AI chatbots?” (Have you used the following AI chatbots?), with answers for work and for leisure.

ICT use in enterprises (table ITAV28) Firm · Statistics Denmark · reference month January of each year, latest January 2026 · Firms, about 4,000 enterprises with 10+ employees in private non-financial industries, excluding mining. Asks whether the enterprise uses any of eight AI technologies; this is the Danish part of the Eurostat survey, already published for 2026. Figures for 2023 to 2025 were revised to the new industry classification (NACE Rev. 2.1), so they may differ from those published earlier.

Cultural Habits Survey (tables KV2AI1 and KV2AI2) Work and private · Statistics Denmark · 2024 and 2025 · Individuals, residents aged 16+; the survey collects about 4,800 responses per quarter, though some questions go to only part of the sample. “In which situations do you typically use artificial intelligence, generative AI tools or language models as a tool?” (several answers possible), and how often in the past 12 months. The frequency categories changed between 2024 and 2025.

title: Country evidence
text:
Finland
Generative AI module, EVA values and attitudes survey Work and private · ETLA · 8 to 21 October 2024 · Individuals, 2,018 people aged 18 to 79. Asks how often people used an AI web application in the last 12 months, and whether they have used AI for a task in their job.

Working Life Barometer 2025 At work · Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, data collected by Statistics Finland · autumn 2025 · Workers, wage earners aged 18 to 64. Asks whether AI technology is used at the respondent’s workplace, and with what effects.

title: Country evidence
text:
Poland
NBP Quick Monitoring report, July 2026 Firm (in Polish, pp. 24-25) · Narodowy Bank Polski · December 2024 (Quick Monitoring survey, 2,490 firms, reported in the January 2025 report, p. 37) and April to May 2026 (NBP Annual Survey, 1,913 firms) · Firms, non-financial enterprises in all sectors except agriculture, forestry and fishing. Asks whether the firm uses AI tools, plans to, sees no use for them, or has not looked into them. NBP notes that large firms are over-represented in its samples and micro firms clearly under-represented, so the shares are likely above those for all firms; the two waves also come from different NBP surveys.

title: Company surveys
text: Surveys run or commissioned by private companies. Most use online panels and loose definitions of “using AI”, and publish little on method, so they are not plotted on the overview. The label after each name says what the AI question covers: use at work, use for work and in private life (asked separately), use for any purpose, or use by the firm.

AWS / Strand Partners
Unlocking Europe’s AI Potential 2026 Firm · Amazon Web Services, fieldwork by Strand Partners · published March 2026, fieldwork dates not stated · Firms, 17,000 business leaders in 17 European countries (14 in the EU). Asks whether the business has adopted AI; exact wording not published.

SD Worx
HR and Payroll Pulse 2026 At work · SD Worx, fieldwork by iVOX · 27 January to 20 February 2026 · Workers and firms, 16,500 employees and 5,936 HR decision-makers in 16 European countries (13 in the EU). Asks whether and how often employees use AI at work; exact wording not published.

title: Company surveys
text:
EY
European AI Barometer 2025 Any purpose · EY · March 2025 · Workers, 4,942 managers and employees in 9 Western European countries (8 in the EU). “Have you ever been involved with Artificial Intelligence (for example ChatGPT, Perplexity, Midjourney) or have you actively used it?”

title: Company surveys
text:
Deloitte
Trust in generative AI: a European perspective Work and private · Deloitte · 28 June to 12 August 2024 · Individuals, 30,252 people aged 16 to 75 in 11 European countries (9 in the EU). “Have you ever used any generative AI tools, or not?”

title: Company surveys
text:
KPMG / University of Melbourne
Trust, attitudes and use of artificial intelligence: a global study 2025 Work and private · University of Melbourne with KPMG · November 2024 to mid-January 2025 · Individuals, 48,340 people in 47 countries (22 in the EU), about 1,000 per country, online panels. “In your personal life (work/studies), how often do you intentionally use AI tools, including generative AI tools?” Regular or semi-regular use means at least every few months. In the Belgium snapshot, 59% of employees say they intentionally use AI at work.

title: Company surveys
text:
PwC
Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 At work · PwC · May and June 2026 · Workers, 49,364 employees in 48 countries and regions, 1,041 in Belgium. Asks whether employees use AI at work; exact wording not published. Figures are from PwC Belgium’s press release.

title: Company surveys
text:
McKinsey
The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI Firm · McKinsey & Company · 4 May to 8 June 2026 · Organisations, as reported by 1,719 respondents at all levels in 97 countries answering an online survey about their organisation; 36% work for organisations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue; weighted by each country’s share of global GDP. Asks whether the organisation regularly uses AI in at least one business function; exact wording not published.
In 2026, 89% of respondents said their organisation regularly uses AI in at least one business function, against 88% in 2025 (Exhibit 1). Among organisations using AI, 44% are scaling it across the enterprise, up from 38%. The 2026 report gives no results by region. The Stanford AI Index 2026 publishes McKinsey’s 2025 results by region (Figure 4.3.2, p. 194): Europe 91%, up from 80% in 2024 and 57% in 2023, although before 2025 McKinsey asked about adoption rather than regular use. Respondents are not a representative sample of firms and any regular use in a single function counts, so the share is far above the 20% of EU enterprises with 10+ employees in Eurostat’s 2025 survey.


The 2026 survey asked respondents whose organisation regularly uses AI how AI changed total employment over the past year: 14% report a decline, less than half the 32% who expected one in the 2025 survey, and two-thirds report little or no change (Exhibit 16).

title: ECB Corporate Telephone Survey
text:
ECB Economic Bulletin 6/2024, Box 4: Findings from a survey of leading
firms on labour market trends and the adoption of generative AI

WhoEuropean Central Bank
When2024
WhereEuro area
SampleFirms46 leading non-financial companies from the ECB’s regular contacts, in a
one-off survey from late May to end-June 2024; not a representative
sample
AI useFirmGenerative AI used operationally by the firm; also the share of
employees using it for work at least once a week
QuestionWhether the firm uses generative AI operationally, since when, what
share of employees use it for work at least once a week, and the main
motivations for adopting it; exact wording not published
DemographicsFirmslarge firms only, sector (broad; manufacturing over-represented)
AdoptionAlmost three-quarters of the 46 firms say they already use generative
AI; these are among the largest firms in the euro area, not a
representative sample

Main aim. To gather early information on business conditions from large euro area
companies the ECB is in regular contact with. This one-off survey of the
same contacts asked about labour market trends and the adoption of
generative AI.Also covers. Labour shortages and difficulty recruiting (scarce skills, changing
skill needs, wages), labour hoarding, hours worked and remote working.
No AI results are published by sector, size or country.
Almost three-quarters of the firms say they already use generative AI in their operations, but about half estimate that no more than 10% of their workforce uses it at least once a week, and only 6% put that share above 25%. Improving employees’ access to information is the main motivation, rated important by more than 90% of users, closely followed by producing content, developing software and engaging with customers; around half of users also see reducing headcount as an important motivation. The firms are among the largest in the euro area, so the share is far above estimates for all firms, and it is not plotted on the overview. The ECB Blog of 28 March 2025 summarises the same results.

title: OECD SME survey
text:

Japan, Korea and the United Kingdom

weighted by number of firms
AI useFirmUse for work by anyone in the firm, including use started by workers
themselves

generative AI for work?”
DemographicsFirmssize class (1, 2-9, 10-49, 50-249), sector, firm age, country, owner’s gender (one-person firms only)
Adoption31% of SMEs across the 7 countries; 38.7% in Germany, 34.1% in Austria,

training for employees, internal guidelines on use, and barriers to
adoption.

The question counts any use by anyone in the firm, including staff using tools on their own initiative, and includes one-person firms, so it is not comparable with Eurostat’s enterprise survey of firms with 10+ employees. It is not plotted on the overview: the measure differs from the other firm surveys, and the 31% headline mixes the three EU countries with four non-EU ones.
